course.title: Practical SQL: Query Real Data
course.description: Write real SQL against a live SQLite database in your browser — SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, aggregates, GROUP BY, and JOINs — every query auto-checked against the correct result, no setup required. SQL dialect and structure informed by the public-domain SQLite documentation (sqlite.org).

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause chooses WHICH COLUMNS a query returns?
questions.explanation: SELECT lists the columns (or expressions) to return; FROM names the table, WHERE filters rows.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters WHICH ROWS are returned?
questions.explanation: WHERE keeps only the rows matching a condition.

questions.prompt: To sort results from largest to smallest by a column, you use…
questions.explanation: ORDER BY col DESC sorts descending; ASC (the default) sorts ascending.

questions.prompt: Which function counts the number of rows in a group?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; SUM() adds up a numeric column.

options: combine rows from two tables by a related key
questions.explanation: A JOIN matches rows across tables on a shared key (e.g. orders.customer_id = customers.id).

questions.prompt: GROUP BY is normally paired with…
options: an aggregate like SUM or COUNT
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups so an aggregate (SUM, COUNT, AVG) is computed per group.

lessons.title: SELECT, FROM, and WHERE
lessons.grammar_note: Text literals go in single quotes in SQL: WHERE city = 'Lisbon'. Double quotes mean an identifier (a column/table name), not a string.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read rows from a table, pick specific columns, and filter with a condition. Warm-up: which clause decides which rows come back — SELECT or WHERE?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A query has three core parts. SELECT lists the columns you want (or * for all). FROM names the table. WHERE filters to the rows that match a condition. So SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lisbon' returns just the name column, only for customers whose city is Lisbon. Conditions use =, <>, <, >, <=, >=, and combine with AND/OR. Text is wrapped in single quotes; numbers are bare.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Given a customers table (id, name, city): SELECT * FROM customers returns every column and row. SELECT name, city FROM customers returns two columns. SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lisbon' returns only Lisbon customers' names. SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id > 2 returns rows with id 3 and up. Combine: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lisbon' AND id < 3.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For customers(id, name, city): 1) Write a query for all columns of every customer. 2) Return just the name column. 3) Return names of customers in 'Porto'. 4) Return all customers with id at least 3. Answers: 1) SELECT * FROM customers; 2) SELECT name FROM customers; 3) SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Porto'; 4) SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id >= 3;

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using double quotes for a text value — 'Lisbon' is a string, "Lisbon" is read as a column name. Mistake: forgetting WHERE and returning the whole table. Exit: (a) Which clause picks columns? (b) Which clause filters rows? Answers: SELECT; WHERE.

body.prompt: Return the name of every customer who lives in Lisbon. (Return just the name column.)
body.instructions: The database is seeded for you — open the schema to see the tables. Write your query and Run. The first run loads the in-browser SQLite engine once.
body.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lisbon';

lessons.title: ORDER BY and LIMIT
lessons.grammar_note: ORDER BY runs after WHERE; LIMIT runs last. So the order is: filter rows, sort them, then keep the top N.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sort query results and keep only the top rows. Warm-up: how do you sort from highest to lowest?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: ORDER BY col sorts the result by a column, ascending by default; add DESC for descending. LIMIT n keeps only the first n rows after sorting — perfect for 'top N' questions. You can sort by multiple columns: ORDER BY city ASC, amount DESC sorts by city, breaking ties by amount.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Given orders(id, customer_id, product, amount): SELECT product, amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC lists the most expensive orders first. Add LIMIT 3 to keep only the three priciest. SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 1 returns the single cheapest order. Ties are broken by whatever you list next in ORDER BY.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For orders(id, customer_id, product, amount): 1) Sort all orders by amount ascending. 2) Return the top 2 orders by amount (highest first). 3) Return the single most expensive order's product. Answers: 1) SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY amount; 2) SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 2; 3) SELECT product FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1;

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting LIMIT to pick the 'best' rows without ORDER BY — without sorting, the rows kept are arbitrary. Mistake: writing DESC before the column. Exit: (a) What keeps only the first N rows? (b) What sorts descending? Answers: LIMIT N; ORDER BY col DESC.

body.prompt: Return the product and amount of the 3 most expensive orders, highest amount first.
body.instructions: Order matters here — the rows must come back sorted from highest amount to lowest. Return the product and amount columns.
body.solution: SELECT product, amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3;

lessons.title: Aggregates, GROUP BY, and JOIN
lessons.grammar_note: When you GROUP BY a column, every other column in SELECT must be either that grouping column or wrapped in an aggregate (SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Summarize rows with aggregates, group them by a column, and combine two tables with a JOIN. Warm-up: which function adds up a numeric column?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Aggregates collapse many rows into one value: COUNT(*) counts rows, SUM(amount) totals a column, AVG, MIN, MAX do the rest. GROUP BY col computes an aggregate per group — SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY city gives a count per city. A JOIN combines tables on a related key: SELECT ... FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id matches each order to its customer. Aliases (c, o) keep column references short and unambiguous.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders totals every order. SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id totals per customer. Joining for names: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name gives each customer's total spend. SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.city counts orders per city.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For customers(id,name,city) and orders(id,customer_id,product,amount): 1) Total of all order amounts. 2) Number of orders per customer_id. 3) Each customer name with their total spend (JOIN + GROUP BY). Answers: 1) SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders; 2) SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; 3) SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name;

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: selecting a non-aggregated column that is not in GROUP BY. Mistake: forgetting the ON condition in a JOIN, which pairs every row with every other. Exit: (a) What does GROUP BY do? (b) What connects two tables in a JOIN? Answers: computes an aggregate per group; the ON condition matching a shared key.

body.prompt: Return each customer's name alongside the total amount they have spent across all their orders. Use a JOIN and GROUP BY.
body.instructions: Join customers to orders on the customer id, group by the customer, and SUM the amount. Row order does not matter here.
body.solution: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name;

questions.prompt: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lisbon' returns…
options: just the name column for Lisbon customers
questions.explanation: SELECT name limits to one column; WHERE limits to Lisbon rows.

questions.prompt: To keep only the top 3 rows after sorting, add…
questions.explanation: SQLite uses LIMIT n; ORDER BY must come first to define 'top'.

options: one number: the total of all amounts
questions.explanation: SUM aggregates the whole column into a single total.

questions.prompt: In SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) ... GROUP BY c.name, the amount is summed…
questions.explanation: GROUP BY c.name computes the SUM within each customer.

options: how rows in the two tables are matched
questions.explanation: ON gives the matching condition, e.g. o.customer_id = c.id.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid string literal in SQLite?
questions.explanation: Single quotes denote a string; double quotes/brackets denote identifiers.

body.prompt: Return each city alongside the number of orders placed by customers in that city. Use a JOIN, GROUP BY, and COUNT.
body.instructions: Join orders to their customer to know each order's city, then count orders per city. Row order does not matter.
body.solution: SELECT c.city, COUNT(*) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.city;

body.prompt: Return the single city whose customers have spent the most in total, with its total spend. Return two columns: the city and the total.
body.instructions: Combine everything: JOIN, GROUP BY city, SUM the amounts, ORDER BY the total descending, and LIMIT to 1.
body.starter:
SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.city;
body.solution: SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY SUM(o.amount) DESC LIMIT 1;
